name: PT Buma Internasional Grup Tbk

frontmatter.title: BUMA Internasional Group: fees from coal, debt from a producer
frontmatter.summary: DOID is a coal-mining contractor with producer-sized debt: net debt of US$872.7m, 5.0 our EBITDA. We rate the shares REDUCE with a Rp120 target: the discounted cash flow floors at zero, and the entire positive value is the 15.0% strategic-buyer branch.
thesis: Revenue is a fee for moving rock and coal, not a coal price: the annual report says lower thermal coal prices did not directly reduce revenue but hit customer performance and contract negotiations [S2, p.32], so we model the coal channel as volume and renewal timing — the contract-loss bear — not as a price realisation, and a commodity-producer build would tie revenue to a price the company does not sell at.
The debt is the investment case. FY2025 finance cost of US$91.6m exceeded free cash flow to the firm, and on our forecast the shortfall is refinanced every year rather than repaid [S6].

EBITDA is US$173.8m on the LK's own lines, not the data pack's lower figure: the operating result of US$-68.0m plus total depreciation and amortisation of US$241.8m, which reconciles to the US$175m the company reports [S2, pp.10, 362, 405-407].

The discounted cash flow puts enterprise value at US$6.4m, below net debt, so the equity value floors at zero; the only positive method is the peer EV/EBITDA cross-check, which applies a coal-producer multiple to a contractor, carries a 15.0% weight in the blend and is the entire positive value, the scenario set's probability of the buyer branch [S2].

The market pays Rp150 for an option our probability-weighted scenarios value at Rp120: both the base case and the weighted value sit below the price, and only the bull branch, which needs enterprise value to clear the debt, is above it [S6].
No dividend since the final payment for FY2023, negative book equity from FY2026E and covenants already waived at the balance-sheet date leave no distribution capacity in the base case [S6; F34].

blocks.text: **Correction: the previous version of this update was struck on a rejected exchange rate, and we have reverted it.** The previous version moved the target on the dollar-rupiah placeholder in the Yahoo data pack [S0] — the rate the macro deck's own basis note rejects as stale and offshore. The reviewed onshore close, and the rate the engine now reads, is Rp18,080/USD on 23 October 2026. Reverting the mechanically-driven move is the honest answer: the operating forecast is unchanged, but the target is re-struck at the reviewed rate and the rating is REDUCE at Rp120, -20.2% from the Rp150 price. We also correct the multiple's denominator: it is now applied to EBITDA including the amortisation of mining properties and intangibles, US$173.8m, which is the definition the peer multiples use [S2 pp.406-407; F58]. The two corrections pull in opposite directions and the net is a target below the price. The DCF is untouched: its enterprise value of US$6.4m is still below net debt, the cash-flow branch is still worth zero, and the entire positive value remains the buyer branch.

We update coverage of DOID, the company now called PT BUMA Internasional Grup, at REDUCE with a twelve-month target of Rp120, -20.2% from the Rp150 price. The company is one of the largest coal-mining contractors in Indonesia and has expanded into Australia and the United States, but the equity sits behind a debt load that the operating cash flow does not cover. The valuation is therefore less a view on coal than a view on whether enterprise value can grow faster than the debt.

The business earned US$1,480.3m of revenue in FY2025, down from US$1,756.3m, and reported EBITDA of US$175m, or US$207m before severance costs [S2, p.48]. Finance cost was US$91.6m, more than the EBITDA left after the capital spending the fleet requires [S2]. The group lost US$-127.6m at the net line, and parent book equity is effectively gone: US$51.6m at the last year end and only a few million dollars at the interim balance sheet, against net debt of US$872.7m [S2, S6].

Our valuation mixes two methods that disagree violently. The discounted cash flow, at a cost of capital of 11.7%, produces an enterprise value of US$6.4m, which is less than net debt; limited liability floors the equity value at zero. The EV/EBITDA cross-check, at the peer-median multiple of 5.6, produces Rp526 per share. That cross-check carries a 15.0% weight in the blend of Rp79, because that is the scenario set's probability of the buyer branch, and it is the entire positive value: the DCF floor is zero, so the multiple is one hundred per cent of the value that is above zero. The target of Rp120 is the probability-weighted scenario value after the house liquidity haircut of 10.0% [S0].

A mining contractor is paid a fee per cubic metre of overburden moved or per tonne of coal hauled, usually under a multi-year contract with an escalation clause. The fee covers equipment, fuel, labour and maintenance; the contractor owns the fleet and therefore carries the capital intensity of the mine without owning the reserve. When the mine owner cuts its stripping plan the contractor loses volume, not price, and when fuel or wages rise the contractor absorbs the gap until the contract resets.

What would change the call is not a better coal price by itself. It is a sustained recovery in gross margin, a contract award that lifts volume without new capital, or a capital-structure event that converts debt into something the cash flow can service. Each is possible, and the bull scenario prices a partial version of the first. But the base case holds the FY2025 cost structure in real terms, as the house method requires, and on that basis the equity has no intrinsic value.

DOID began life as a textile company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange and became a coal-mining contractor through the acquisition of PT Bukit Makmur Mandiri Utama, the operating subsidiary still known as BUMA [S2, p.60]. The transformation was completed with the acquisition of Downer's Australian mining-services business, which became BUMA Australia, and more recently with the acquisition of Atlantic Carbon Group, an anthracite producer in Pennsylvania [S2]. The company changed its name to PT BUMA Internasional Grup during the period covered by the annual report, and its shares continue to trade under the old Delta Dunia identity.

The revenue model is a service fee. BUMA removes overburden, drills and blasts, gets coal, hauls it and manages mine infrastructure for the owner, and is paid per unit of work under contracts that typically run for several years [S2]. In FY2025 the company moved 439 million bank cubic metres of overburden, produced 84 million tonnes of coal for its clients and operated at a stripping ratio of 5.2x [S2, p.13]. Both volumes fell from FY2024, when overburden removal was 545 million bcm and coal production 90 million tonnes, because several contracts concluded and rainfall was unusually heavy [S5].

The FY2025 revenue of US$1,480.3m was split across three countries. In the first half of 2026, revenue from Indonesia was US$459.8m, from Australia US$210.7m and from the United States US$22.3m, so the Australian business is roughly a third of the group and the American business is small but growing from the Atlantic Carbon acquisition [S6, p.117]. The customer base is concentrated: the five largest customers produced 78.0% of revenue in that half, led by Indonesia Pratama, TEC Coal, Adaro, Whitehaven and Berau Coal, so the loss of any one of the larger contracts would be material [S6, p.106].

The contract book is long-dated but finite. The Adaro South Tutupan award, which started on 1 April 2026, is expected to deliver 239 million bcm of overburden removal and 44 million tonnes of coal over its term to 31 December 2030 [S4]. The Australian contracts at Blackwater run to mid-2030 and at Goonyella Riverside to September 2027, after which they are renewals rather than backlog [S2, p.49]. At the nine-month stage of 2024 the company described an order book of 12.7 USD bn, tripled by extensions and new wins including an eleven-year extension with a Bayan Group subsidiary and a life-of-mine contract with a Singaraja Putra subsidiary [S5]. That order book is the strongest part of the story, and it is why the revenue base has held up better than the coal price. It is a stock of contracted work, not a growth rate: it is total contract value, several times annual revenue, and it converts into revenue only as the client's mine plan is executed, which is why our forecast lifts revenue with the Adaro ramp and then holds it rather than extrapolating the backlog [S5].

The group also owns assets outside the fee business. Atlantic Carbon Group owns and leases more than 8,000 hectares in Pennsylvania and produces anthracite [S2, p.366], and the company holds 22.6% of its ASX-listed Australian copper and precious-metals associate, of which DOID is the largest shareholder, up from 20.0% at the previous year end [S6, p.67]. Those holdings sit in the investment line of the balance sheet and are added back in our valuation bridge rather than valued on their own cash flows, because the company does not disclose enough to model them separately. The group employed 11,190 people at the last count [S0].

The controlling shareholder is Northstar Tambang Persada, which held 38.2% of the shares at 31 December 2025, down from a little over two fifths a year earlier, with Six Sis and Trimegah Sekuritas the other holders above the reporting threshold [S2, p.88]. Treasury shares and a free float of 45.5% complete the picture [S0]. The controlling stake is large enough that any capital-structure solution — a rights issue, an asset sale or a debt-for-equity swap — is a negotiated outcome with Northstar rather than a market one.

A contractor's contracts are usually priced per unit of work with indexation for fuel, wages and, in some cases, the client's own selling price. Because the contractor supplies the fleet, the balance sheet is heavy with property, plant and equipment that is depreciated over the contract life and must be replaced or rebuilt when contracts are won. Revenue is a function of the client's mine plan and the contractor's win rate, while cost is a function of diesel, tyres, labour and maintenance. The spread between the two is thin and cyclical.

Indonesian coal is a volume business with a policy overlay. The Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources set the 2026 work plan and budget, the RKAB, at 600 million tonnes of national production, but expects actual output of around 720 million tonnes, based on production running at roughly sixty million tonnes a month through the year [S9]. The domestic market obligation requires producers to sell 25.0% of output domestically, and the ministry is reviewing the rule because domestic supply may fall short, with sanctions for producers that miss the obligation [S9]. For a contractor the RKAB matters indirectly: it sets how much rock its clients are permitted to move.

The price backdrop has been two-sided. Thermal coal prices corrected through the period while metallurgical coal and copper rose, and the company states plainly that the fall in thermal prices did not directly reduce its revenue but affected customer performance and contract negotiations, while higher metallurgical and copper prices helped the diversified part of the book [S2, p.32]. That is the clearest statement in the filing of why this is not a producer: the coal price reaches DOID through the client's willingness to strip and through the rate negotiated at contract renewal, not through a realisation per tonne. We therefore put no coal price in the model. The deck's thermal path enters through the volume and renewal assumptions — the contract-loss bear and the revenue-growth path — rather than as a realisation, because the filing says the price did not directly move revenue; if a reader believes the price beta is direct, the bear case is the honest place to test it, and the sensitivity table shows that even a large operating improvement does not lift the floored DCF.

Volume, not price, is the operating driver, and volume has been falling. FY2025 overburden removal of 439 million bcm was below FY2024's 545 million bcm, and coal production of 84 million tonnes was below the prior year's 90 million tonnes [S2, p.13]. The company attributed part of the decline to weather: rainfall was up by more than a third in Indonesia and by almost a third in Australia in 2024, and the Australian overburden decline followed the conclusion of contracts at Broadmeadow, Commodore and Saraji [S5]. Weather is a real variable in this business, and it is one the company cannot hedge.

Competition is concentrated among a small number of Indonesian contractors with national fleets. BUMA is one of the largest by volume, alongside the other listed contractor in the sector, and the barriers are the capital cost of a fleet, the safety and operating record needed to win tenders from the large mine owners, and the working-capital capacity to carry receivables through a contract ramp [S2]. The moat is real but narrow: a contractor with a good safety record and available fleet can win work, and the customer can move the work to another contractor at the end of a term, which is what happened at several Australian sites in FY2024 [S5].

The five forces are mixed. Supplier power is high on fuel and tyres, which are globally priced and, in Indonesia, partly administered; buyer power is high because a handful of mine owners award the contracts and the top five customers are 78.0% of revenue [S6, p.106]; the threat of new entrants is moderate because a fleet is expensive but not scarce; substitution is low in the short run because the work has to be done physically; and rivalry is intense at contract renewal, where the incumbent's cost base is visible to the client. The result is a business that earns a thin spread over a heavy asset base, which is exactly what the margin history shows.

Coal contractors sit between the mine owner and the equipment manufacturers. Contracts are usually awarded on a combination of rate, fleet availability, safety record and financial standing, and the owner retains the right to re-tender at the end of the term. Because the contractor's assets are mobile, the fleet can be redeployed between sites, which limits the value of incumbency but also limits the client's ability to squeeze the contractor without risking the mine plan. The sector is therefore cyclical with coal volumes and capital-intensive through the cycle.

The policy overlay cuts both ways. A higher RKAB supports volumes for the contractor's clients, but the DMO review and the possibility of tighter domestic-supply rules could redirect coal away from the export mines that generate the highest stripping volumes [S9]. Royalty changes affect the producer's economics and therefore its willingness to strip, not the contractor's fee directly, which is why we do not model a royalty line. The energy transition is a slow negative for thermal coal volumes and a slower positive for the metallurgical and copper exposure that the company has acquired; neither is a base-case driver over our forecast horizon.

Revenue fell from US$1,553.7m in FY2022 to US$1,756.3m in FY2024 and US$1,480.3m in FY2025, -15.7% year on year as contracts concluded and volumes fell [S2]. The profitability trend is steeper than the revenue trend. Gross margin fell from 13.1% in FY2022 and 13.4% in FY2023 to 8.7% in FY2024 and 2.8% in FY2025, and reported EBITDA fell by more than two fifths, to US$175m, or US$207m before severance costs [S2, p.48]. The FY2024 margin was flattered by a strong first half, and the FY2025 number absorbs severance and other one-off costs.

Two of those one-offs are named and sized in the notes, and they explain why the net loss is so much larger than the operating loss. The group charged US$21.0m of allowance for impaired trade receivables and US$11.4m of impairment against fixed assets through other expenses in FY2025 [S2, p.405], and the board's review attributes the net loss to the provision against Australian receivables and to the write-down of the US operations [S2, p.35]. Both sit below the operating line, so neither is in the EBITDA we capitalise; the provision is a credit loss on work already done and the impairment is a write-down of assets the company carries at recoverable value, and we treat both as non-recurring without pretending they did not happen.

Two restatements matter. First, depreciation: the data pack carries a depreciation line of a few million dollars for the early years, which is not the real charge. The notes to the FY2025 accounts show depreciation charged to profit or loss of US$234.7m in FY2025 and US$255.4m in FY2024, split between cost of revenues and operating expenses [S2, p.362]. We use those figures, and the effect is to rebuild the cost base and the EBITDA margin; a cash cost calibrated off the pack's depreciation line would be wrong by an order of magnitude.

Second, the cost of debt. Finance cost was US$91.6m in FY2025 and US$102.7m in FY2024, against a blended debt balance above a billion dollars, a cash cost of roughly nine per cent rather than the lower figure implied by the pack [S2]. The bank facilities were priced at between six and seven and a quarter per cent at the interim date, with the notes and leases above that, so we hold a blended cost of debt of 8.5% in the forecast [S6, pp.75, 80].

The EBITDA we publish is US$173.8m, and the reconciliation matters because the multiple is applied to it. The LK's operating result of US$-68.0m [F43] plus total depreciation and amortisation of US$241.8m [F58] gives that number: the US$234.7m fixed-asset depreciation charge [F7] plus the amortisation of mining properties and intangibles charged in cost of revenues and operating expenses. That is within a fraction of a million dollars of the US$175m the company reports, and it matches the denominator the peer multiples use, which is earnings before depreciation and amortisation [S2, pp.405-407]. The data pack prints a lower operating result because it folds the Australian receivable provision into operating cost, which the LK does not. We apply the peer multiple to the LK line, which keeps the provision and the impairment out of the capitalised base and keeps the severance charge in it, even though the company strips severance out to reach US$207m. That is the conservative end of the range: on the company's ex-severance figure the cross-check would be worth more than twice as much.

The cash flow statement explains the balance sheet. Capital expenditure was US$177.6m in FY2025 and free cash flow to the firm was US$62.8m, positive but small relative to the interest bill [S2]. In the first half of 2026 the company generated US$63.8m of operating cash flow on US$692.8m of revenue, spent US$49.2m of cash on fixed assets and reported EBITDA of US$69.0m, an improvement on the prior year despite lower revenue [S3, S6]. Management attributes the improvement to workforce optimisation, maintenance and fuel efficiency, and says that excluding the fuel-price increase EBITDA would have been higher still [S3]. The improvement is real, but it is an efficiency story on a small base, not a recovery in the spread.

The balance sheet is where the risk lives. Net debt was US$872.7m at the FY2025 year end, or 5.0 times EBITDA on our numbers and 5.1x on the company's, which is above the covenant level of three and a half times that the company discloses [S2, S6, p.77]. The year-end figure nets cash plus other financial assets; the interim figure used in the valuation bridge nets cash only, and the two definitions differ by well inside five per cent of net debt, so we treat the comparison as like-for-like and use the interim measure throughout the valuation. The company obtained waivers of the debt-service and leverage covenants for the end-2025 and mid-2026 test dates, which means the lenders have already had to accommodate the company once [S6, p.77]. Book equity was US$51.6m at the year end and only a few million dollars at the interim date, with a negative minority interest, so the parent equity cushion is effectively gone [S6].

Our forecast holds the FY2025 cost structure in real terms and lets revenue follow the contract arithmetic. Revenue is -1.0% in FY2026E, then grows at 4.0% as the Adaro contract annualises, before stepping down to the low single digits [S4]. Gross margin is held at the FY2025 level at FY2025 fuel costs and then adjusted by the Brent link, which produces a margin of 1.8% in FY2026E, in line with the first half [S6]. Depreciation is 14.5% of revenue, below FY2025 because the asset base is smaller after disposals, and capex is 7.5% in FY2026E rising to 10.2%, which is about seven tenths of depreciation. In dollars that is US$109.9m and US$155.5m against the US$177.6m spent in FY2025: we assume the fleet is maintained rather than replaced, because the first half of 2026 ran at US$49.2m of cash capex [F35], roughly half the prior-year half. This is the parameter the case leans on, and it is below the last full-year actual; a return to the FY2025 ratio would remove the bull case's capex saving, which is the main thing that turns its DCF equity positive.

On those inputs EBITDA is US$143.7m in FY2026E and US$156.0m in FY2027E, while finance cost rises to US$94.5m and then above a hundred million dollars a year as the debt is refinanced [S6]. The group stays loss-making: net income is US$-158.5m in FY2026E and US$-161.0m in FY2027E. Free cash flow to the firm is US$23.6m in FY2026E and US$-3.0m in FY2027E as capex steps up, well below the interest bill, so free cash flow to equity is negative in every year after the first and the company must roll its maturities rather than repay them [S6].

That is the central forecast result: net new borrowing of roughly seventy million dollars a year keeps the cash balance near the interim level, but debt rises from US$1,111.8m at the FY2025 year end to US$1,478.8m by FY2030E and US$1,882.2m by FY2035E, and book equity becomes steadily more negative [S6]. We do not assume a default and we do not assume a rescue equity issue; we assume the company refinances at its current blended cost, which is the most likely path while the lenders are cooperative. A reader who thinks the lenders will stop cooperating should read the bear case as the binding one.

The earnings-quality screens are unambiguous. Accruals are heavy relative to cash because depreciation is larger than EBITDA, a sign of an asset base being consumed faster than the cash generation supports; a receivable book that required a US$21.0m provision in FY2025 is the clearest evidence that the revenue is not all collectable, and the customer base that produced it is concentrated in five names [S2, p.405; S6, p.106]; working capital has been a source of cash for two years as receivables ran down, which cannot repeat indefinitely; and the one-offs in the half-year — a land-sale gain, a foreign-exchange gain and a fair-value loss on the Australian mining stake — are exactly the items the company itself labels non-operational [S3]. We exclude them from the forecast and do not capitalise them [S2, S3].

The method set follows the business, not the industry code. DOID is listed in the coal sector, but the fee business is the revenue: it does not receive a coal price for the work it does, and the one place it does sell a tonne, the Atlantic Carbon anthracite operation in Pennsylvania, was a low single-digit share of interim revenue [S6, p.117]. A commodity-producer build would tie revenue to a Newcastle price and apply a royalty schedule to service revenue, which is why we use the corporate template with revenue growth, a gross margin and a Brent cost link, and the contractor method map: discounted cash flow as the primary method, EV/EBITDA as a cross-check [S2, p.60]. The multiple source is the peer median rather than the company's own five-year average, because the company's own history includes a year in which depressed EBITDA produced a multiple in the high teens that says nothing about today.

The cost of capital is built from a dollar risk-free rate of 4.8%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and an Indonesia country premium of 2.5%, with an unlevered beta of 1.00 taken from the industry regression median and relevered at the engine's leverage cap of 2.00 times to 2.56. That gives a cost of equity of 24.6% and, with a 33.3% equity weight, a weighted cost of capital of 11.7%. Two corrections are built into those numbers. The engine prices the debt leg at the macro corporate spread of 6.8%, which is well below what DOID actually pays: the bank facilities were priced at between six and seven and a quarter per cent, the 2025 bond series runs from a one-year tranche at six and three quarters per cent to a five-year tranche at eight and three quarters per cent [F53], and the FY2025 finance cost of US$91.6m on opening debt of about a billion dollars implies a blended rate near nine per cent [S2, p.72; F9]. Rather than leave the gap, we add a 2.6% premium to the cost of equity, which lifts the WACC by the same amount as repricing the debt at the company's blended 8.5% at the engine's weights [S6, pp.75, 80; F49, F50]. The leverage cap, by contrast, flatters the equity by holding the equity weight above the market's; the two corrections run in opposite directions, and we do not claim the net discount rate is generous.

The discounted cash flow produces an enterprise value of US$6.4m. The terminal value is negative, because free cash flow in the terminal year is negative — fleet replacement absorbs the EBITDA the business earns — so we do not quote a terminal-value share of value: there is no positive continuing value to decompose. Net debt at the interim balance sheet, the minority interest and the investments are then bridged to equity, and the result is negative. Because equity holders have limited liability, the engine floors the DCF equity value at zero. That is not a modelling artefact: it is the statement that, on our cash flows and our cost of capital, the enterprise is worth less than the debt, and the equity is a call option on the difference.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check gives a different answer. At the peer-median multiple of 5.6 times the restated FY2025A EBITDA of US$173.8m — the LK operating line plus total depreciation and amortisation, not the company's ex-severance measure and not the data pack's lower figure [F43, F58] — the enterprise value covers net debt and leaves Rp526 per share after the investment add-back. The median is an effective eighteen of the twenty-five names listed: seven carry no positive LTM EBITDA and are screened out, and the two names bracketing the median are ARII and BSSR; dropping both brackets and the contractor KKGI leaves a median above the published one, so the multiple is not propped by two names. The contractor sub-set — DEWA, KKGI and MYOH — medians below the producer set and is shown as a cross-check rather than used: three names spanning a six-fold range, one of them a distressed outlier, are not a benchmark a median can carry. The P/E cross-check is unavailable because the company is loss-making, so the engine uses two live methods with weights we set at 85.0% for the DCF and 15.0% for the multiple. The blended value is Rp79 per share, which rolls forward at the cost of equity to Rp98 on the base case, and the published target of Rp120 is the probability-weighted scenario value after the house liquidity haircut of 10.0% [S0]. Two sensitivities sit behind that number and we disclose both. The first is the exchange rate: the peer median is a dollar multiple struck on rupiah market caps, so a materially stronger rupiah lifts the target through the HOLD boundary and a weaker one takes it to SELL — the rating is not FX-neutral, and we judge it at the reviewed onshore rate of Rp18,080. The second is the tail weight: moving three points of probability from the bear to the bull leaves the rating unchanged, and it would take a larger reallocation than the house minimum tail to move it, which is why we do not present REDUCE as a comfortable call. The base branch on its own, the most likely path at 60.0%, is worth less than the price.

The two methods disagree by more than the house tolerance, and the reason matters. The peer multiple is a coal-producer multiple: producers convert a much larger share of EBITDA into free cash flow because their capex is a smaller fraction of the revenue that generates it. DOID spends between three quarters and all of its EBITDA on capital expenditure to keep the fleet running [S2], so the cash that a buyer of the equity actually receives is a small fraction of the EBITDA to which the multiple is applied. The DCF captures that; the multiple does not. We keep the multiple at 15.0% of the value for a specific reason: it is what a strategic buyer of the fleet and the contract book might pay, and it is the level at which the market transacts. The blend is a probability statement, not an average of two estimates of the same thing: the weight is the scenario set's probability of the buyer branch, the DCF is the binding value in the other 85.0%, and the reader who rejects the buyer branch should read the value as the floor. The consequence is blunt and we state it: every positive number in the base case comes from that buyer branch, because the DCF floors at zero, so the published value is an option on a buyer, not a stand-alone fundamental value.

The sensitivity table has to be read with the business model in mind, and this time both grids say the same thing. The first varies the cost of capital and terminal growth against the DCF value per share, and every cell is zero: across a plausible band of discount rates the enterprise value stays below net debt, so limited liability holds the equity at the floor and the discount rate cannot rescue it. The second varies revenue growth and gross margin against the twelve-month value, and it is completely flat at the cross-check value: even the top corner — four points more growth and two points more margin in every year — does not lift the DCF enterprise value through net debt. The operating case on its own cannot rescue the equity; the bull scenario needs the capital-spending cut as well, which is why we treat it as an option rather than a forecast. It is a step function, not a slope, and it is the mathematical expression of the leverage.

A reverse DCF is not available: the price is not bracketed, because the floored DCF value is zero across the plausible range of growth, margin and discount rate, so the engine reports that it cannot solve for the price. What the price does imply is visible in the cross-check. At Rp150 the market is capitalising the enterprise a little below the peer median, which requires either a permanent improvement in cash conversion, a lower cost of capital than the debt itself carries, or a buyer who values the fleet and the contract book above their cash flows [S0, S2]. The first is the bull case; the second is not available to a company with this leverage; the third is a control outcome, not a base case.

The dominant risk is refinancing. The company must roll maturities every year because free cash flow to equity is negative, and it has already needed covenant waivers for two test dates [S6, p.77]. The disclosed maturity calendar is not comfortable. The syndicated bank facility matures five and three-quarter years after the first utilisation of each tranche, and the first drawdown was at the end of December 2023, which sets a refinancing date in 2029 [S6, p.75; F51]; the Muamalat facility matures in 2028 [F52]; the insurance funding agreement with Clearmatch matures in April 2027; the First National Bank facility matures on 1 April 2030; and the sukuk and bonds total US$185.0m gross, of which US$39.3m is current [S6, pp.69, 75, 81; F50, F54]. The near maturities are therefore the current bond portion and the insurance facility, while the syndicated loan, which is almost all of the US$770.3m of bank loans, is the one that sets the refinancing date. If the lenders tighten, the equity is diluted or extinguished before the operating story has time to improve. That is a dated risk and it dominates every other consideration in the report. It is also the risk the scenario table cannot price: the engine has no distinct default branch, so the bear prices the operating recession that would precede a default, and a default itself — which would extinguish the equity — is a tail beyond the table and outside the target. That omission makes the target, if anything, high, which reinforces rather than weakens the rating.

The second risk is customer concentration. The five largest customers are 78.0% of revenue, and the largest is a single mine owner whose contract is priced on a rate that is renegotiated [S6, p.106]. A contract loss or a client cutting its stripping plan reduces volume immediately, and the fleet dedicated to the contract cannot be redeployed without cost. The third is cost: fuel is a large direct line, and although part of the increase passes into rates, the pass-through is lagged [S3, S6]. The fourth is weather, which reduced volumes in FY2024 and is outside management's control [S5]. The fifth is currency: revenue and debt are mostly in dollars while the shares and the target are in rupiah, so a weaker rupiah helps the translated target and hurts the dollar cost of local inputs at the same time [S0].

The upside risks are real but narrower than the asset base suggests. A sustained fall in Brent would restore margin faster than the base case assumes, and a new contract award would add volume without proportional capital. The disposal route is weaker than it looks: the associate stake is carried at US$123.4m of equity-method book, the company now owns 22.6% of the ASX-listed copper and precious-metals miner against 20.0% a year earlier, and it added to the position during 2026 rather than selling, buying US$33.1m of additional shares; the Atlantic Carbon land carries no disclosed valuation and the US assets were written down by US$11.4m in FY2025 [S6, pp.4, 67; S2, p.405]. A sale would reduce net debt, but it would also remove the investment add-back that is the difference between a positive and a negative bull-case equity value. We keep both holdings at book in the bridge and assume no disposal.

Our scenarios are mirrored on revenue growth and gross margin, and the table is best read as two states of the capital structure rather than three forecasts of the coal cycle. In the bear case clients cut their stripping plans and the Adaro ramp stalls, revenue falls four points a year against plan, margin gives back two points and the lenders roll the syndicated facility only at a higher margin. On top of that operating decline the bear carries a contract-loss shock: one of the top five customers — 78.0% of revenue between them [F26], with Adaro at 239 million bcm and 44 million tonnes a year to 31 December 2030 [F27, F28] — does not renew or cuts its stripping plan, taking a further six points a year off revenue. That is a one-sided shock and we justify it as such: the concentration is disclosed, the 2030 cliff is dated, and no award of comparable size is disclosed on the upside to mirror it. This is a severe operating recession, not a default: a default would extinguish the equity, and because the engine cannot price a distinct default branch it is a tail beyond the table and not in the target. The engine floors the DCF at zero in both the bear and the base, and the peer multiple is a static input applied to FY2025A EBITDA that no scenario override can move, so the two rows carry the same value: the operating shocks move only the DCF, which is already out of the money, and both rows carry the same 15.0% buyer option. That identity is an engine limitation, not a forecast that the two states are equivalent, and we do not read the bear row as a separate recovery. The base carries 60.0% of the mass and is the most likely path, the bear carries 25.0% and the bull 15.0%.

In the bull case the Adaro ramp and the first-half cost programme hold, new awards extend the book, Brent falls along the deck and capex runs below maintenance, so the equity is worth the multiple and more. Even there the DCF enterprise value does not clear net debt — it comes within a twentieth of it — and the positive equity exists only because the associate stake is added at book, which makes the investment line load-bearing rather than incidental. The bull also leans on the capex parameter, and we state the knife-edge plainly: its capital spending is a fifth below the base's normalised ratio, which is still above the US$49.2m the company actually spent in the first half of 2026, about seven per cent of revenue [S6 p.10; F35], so it is not a below-maintenance assumption; but any capex multiplier above the one we use floors the bull's DCF and takes the bull row back to the base value. The bull is therefore a tail that only pays if the fleet is run at the current spending discipline while revenue grows, not the anchor of the target: a minority of the probability mass, and the base case, the most likely path, is below the price. The weighted value is Rp133 per share and Rp120 after the liquidity haircut, and the expected return is -20.2%; the base-case value is Rp98 before the haircut, also below the price. The rating is REDUCE because the most likely path and the probability-weighted value point the same way, not because the tail carries it.

The signposts we will watch are the covenant test dates, the quarterly cash-flow statement, the net-debt-to-EBITDA ratio, the overburden volume in the quarterly disclosures now that the monthly production report has been discontinued [S5], and any announcement on the maturity profile or a capital raise. A refinancing that extends maturities without adding debt would remove the binary risk and change the rating even without an improvement in the operating case.

The controlling shareholder is Northstar Tambang Persada with 38.2% at the last year end, alongside Six Sis and Trimegah Sekuritas above the reporting threshold, and the board includes a shareholder representative with a personal holding [S2, p.88]. The free float is 45.5% and treasury shares remain from the buyback, so the effective float is smaller than the headline [S0]. There is no indication of a change-of-control process, and the ownership structure means any equity issuance would be negotiated with the controlling holder rather than placed in the market.

The audit is signed by KAP Aria Kanaka & Rekan, a member of Forvis Mazars, and the opinion on the consolidated accounts is unmodified [S2]. The interim accounts are unaudited but reviewed, and the company discloses the covenant waivers in the notes rather than in the front section, which is where a reader should look for them [S6, p.77]. Related-party transactions are disclosed in the notes and are not material to the operating story; the Australian mining stake is an investment, not a trading relationship [S2].

The dividend record is the clearest governance signal. The last distribution was the final dividend for FY2023, paid in July 2024, and there has been no dividend for FY2024 or FY2025 [S2, p.152; F34]. With net debt above five times EBITDA, covenants waived and negative parent equity, there is no capacity for a distribution, and we model none through FY2030E [S6]. A resumption of the dividend would be a genuine signal that the balance sheet has been repaired.

On ESG, the company's exposures are the physical and social footprint of contract mining: safety, dust and emissions from a diesel fleet, land rehabilitation at closed sites, and community relations in the areas where it operates [S2]. The annual report discloses safety and community programmes, and the fleet is the main source of scope-one emissions. The energy transition is a structural negative for thermal coal volumes over the long run, partially offset by the metallurgical and copper exposure acquired with the Australian mining stake and Atlantic Carbon. The company is not a konglo name: there is no group structure of the kind the house screen looks for, and no index-deletion or free-float deadline applies.

The dated catalysts are the quarterly and half-year reports, each of which carries a covenant test, and the full-year results in the first quarter of 2027, when the company will disclose the FY2026 outturn and any dividend decision [S6]. The Adaro contract ramp through 2026 and the first full year in 2027 is the main operating catalyst, and its expiry at the end of 2030 is the main long-dated one [S4]. Any announcement on refinancing, asset sales or a capital raise is a catalyst in its own right because it addresses the binary risk [S6].

Between reports we monitor a short list: overburden volume and strip ratio, because they drive revenue and cost together; gross margin, because it is the swing factor in the equity value; operating cash flow against capex, because that is the refinancing need; net debt and covenant headroom; the Brent price, because it sets the fuel cost; and the rupiah, because it translates the dollar value into the target [S2, S3, S6]. The monthly production report that used to give a high-frequency read on volume was discontinued after December 2024, so the quarterly disclosure is now the only operating data point [S5].

Free cash flow no longer covers interest [S6], and the lenders roll the syndicated facility that matures 69 months after first utilisation [F51] only at a higher margin, so the cost of capital the equity bears rises. This is a severe operating recession, not a default: a default would extinguish the equity, but the engine cannot price a distinct default branch, so the branch is valued on the DCF floor plus the same static buyer option carried in every branch. The table row is therefore the floor of the operating range, not a separate bear-case recovery.

bull.narrative: The Adaro ramp and the 1H2026 cost programme hold, new awards extend the book, Brent falls along the deck and capex runs a fifth below the base's normalised ratio — which is still ABOVE the 7.1% of revenue the company actually spent in 1H2026 [F35, S6 p.10], so the bull does not assume capital spending below the observed run-rate — adding four points a year to revenue and two points to gross margin. The DCF enterprise value comes within about one twentieth of net debt but does not clear it; the equity turns positive only because the associate stake is added at book, not because the cash flows repay the debt.

12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 1H2026 revenue was US$692.8m, 5.1% below 1H2025's US$730.2m [F20, F22, S6], and LTM revenue is US$1,442.9m (data pack), so FY2026E is set at -1.0%: the Adaro South Tutupan contract started on 1 April 2026 and adds 50.5 million bcm and 9.3 Mt a year at full rate over its term to 2030 [F27, F28, S4], which offsets the contract ramp-downs that cut FY2025 revenue 16%. FY2027E +4.0% carries the first full year of Adaro plus the Blackwater (to June 2030), Goonyella Riverside (to September 2027) and Whitehaven extensions [S2, p.49]; FY2028E-FY2030E step down to +3.0%, +2.5% and +2.0%. We do not translate the US$12.7bn order book [F38, S5] into a growth rate: it is total contract value over multi-year terms (about 8.6x FY2025 revenue), while annual revenue is set by each client's yearly mine plan, and the awards disclosed since it was published are already in the forecast. The deceleration is therefore contract arithmetic on the disclosed terms, not a statement that the backlog has run off. No formal volume or revenue guidance is published. LT 2.0% is the macro deck's long-run USD inflation, not real growth.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross margin was 2.81% (revenue US$1,480.3m, COGS US$1,438.7m) [F1, F3, S2] and 1H2026 was 1.76% (US$692.8m against US$680.7m) [F20, S6], the trough after 8.7% in FY2024 and 13.4% in FY2023. The input is stated AT FY2025 BASE FUEL COSTS, as the template requires: 2.8% reproduces FY2025 and, after the Brent link below (FY2026E 96.0 vs the FY2025 average of 68.1), lands at the 1H2026 run rate rather than assuming a recovery. We do not add a margin-expansion story: management's cost programme (workforce optimisation, fuel efficiency, maintenance) is already visible in the 1H2026 EBITDA recovery to US$69m [F21, S3], which the link and opex inputs carry. Costs stay at the last actual in real terms thereafter.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Fuel is a direct cost line of US$153.4m in 1H2026, 22.5% of the US$680.7m cost of revenues [S6, p.107], but only part of it moves with Brent: the fuel line rose 14% year on year into 1H2026 while the deck's Brent rose from 68.1 to 96.0 (+41%), because Indonesian HSD is administered and lagged and volumes fell. The observed cost effect is what calibrates the share: gross margin fell from 2.81% in FY2025 to 1.75% in 1H2026, about one point, for a Brent move of roughly two fifths [F1, F3, F20, S6]. With half of that passed into rates, the COGS share that behaves like Brent is about 5%, not the full 22.5% fuel line, which would overstate the cost swing in both directions.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: The fuel line in cost of revenues rose to US$153.4m in 1H2026 from US$134.4m in 1H2025, a US$19.1m increase [F47, F48, S6 p.107]. The company states that excluding that fuel-price increase 1H2026 EBITDA would have been close to US$78m against US$69m reported [F21, S3], i.e. about US$9m of the US$19.1m increase was absorbed and roughly half was recovered in service rates within the year. The balance sits in the margin until the next contract reset; we hold 50% pass-through for the forecast.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating expenses were US$108.7m, 7.34% of revenue [F5, F1, S2]; 1H2026 was US$44.9m, 6.48% of revenue [S6, p.7]. We hold the nine-month run-rate at 6.5% rather than the FY2025 ratio, because the FY2025 number carried severance and impairment-related charges that the company identifies as one-off (EBITDA ex-severance US$207m) [F31, S2]. No cost-cut is assumed beyond the observed level.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A charged to profit or loss was US$234.7m (US$231.9m in COGS and US$2.8m in opex) [F7, S2 p.362], 15.9% of revenue; FY2024 was US$255.4m [F8]. 1H2026 depreciation fell with the asset base after disposals and impairments (US$96.8m in COGS plus US$1.3m in opex and US$1.4m amortisation), about 14.4% of revenue [S6, pp.63,107]. We hold 14.5% for the forecast, below FY2025 because the fleet base is smaller, and never calibrate a cash cost off the Yahoo D&A line, which is a fraction of the real charge.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 gross capex was US$177.6m (12.0% of revenue), including US$169.5m of fixed assets [F18, S2 p.72], US$6.4m of mining properties and US$1.7m of intangibles; FY2024 was US$175.5m (10.0%) on a D&A charge of US$255.4m [F8, F19], and FY2023 was US$131.8m (7.2%). Capex has therefore run at 69% of D&A in FY2024 (175.5/255.4) and 73% in FY2025 (177.6/241.8 of total depreciation and amortisation), not at the 58.6% the previous version of this file implied: 8.5% of revenue is not seventy per cent of a 14.5% D&A charge, 10.15% is. We start FY2026E at 7.5%, close to the 1H2026 fixed-asset run-rate of 7.1% of revenue [F35, S6 p.10], then normalise to 10.2%, which is seventy per cent of the 14.5% D&A rate and US$150-160m a year against the FY2025 actual of US$177.6m for the same fleet. Holding capex at 8.5% would have understated the cash cost of the fleet by about US$24m a year and flattered free cash flow.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 net working capital was US$77.8m on revenue of US$1,480.3m, 5.3%; 1H2026 was US$65.8m on US$692.8m, 9.5% on a seasonal low revenue base [S0, S6]. We hold 6.0% of revenue, close to the FY2025 level and above the FY2024 7.6% peak, with no unsourced working-capital release.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Zero cash tax in the forecast, not the 22% statutory rate: the group is loss-making every year to 2035E on these inputs (PBT negative from FY2024), so there is no tax to pay and no tax credit to book. Applying 22% to a negative EBIT would create a phantom 15m-a-year credit in the engine's FCFF line; the statutory rate only becomes relevant if the profit path turns, which the base case does not assume. Accumulated tax losses are not capitalised as an asset.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance cost was US$91.6m on opening debt of US$1,002.7m (9.1%); FY2024 was US$102.7m on US$1,190.7m (8.6%) [F9, F10, S2]. The bank facilities carried 7.64%-8.39% at 30 June 2026 [S6, p.80] and the Senior Notes and leases sit above that, so 8.5% is the blended run-rate, not the Yahoo 7.49%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 finance income was US$4.1m on opening cash of US$211.4m, 1.9% [S0, S2]; 1H2026 interest received was US$1.8m. We hold 2.0%.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: 1H2026 was a net repayment year: US$57.5m of bank draws against US$52.3m bank repayments, US$31.9m of Senior Notes repaid, US$12.9m of long-term debt and US$21.8m of leases, a net outflow of about US$61m [S6, p.10]. That repayment was funded from a cash balance of US$211.4m at the start of the year, which fell to US$158.5m by 30 June 2026 [S6]. Repeating it is not available: on the forecast the annual interest bill of roughly US$90m exceeds FCFF of US$24-29m, so free cash flow to equity is negative and the company must refinance rather than deleverage. We therefore model net new borrowing of about US$70-75m a year, which holds cash near the 30 June 2026 level and rolls the shortfall, with debt roughly flat in nominal terms. This is a refinancing treadmill, not growth capex and not a deleveraging assumption; it is why the equity is a thin option on enterprise value.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 other income of US$58.3m and other expenses of US$57.5m net to US$0.8m [S2, p.68]; we hold zero and do not capitalise the 1H2026 land-sale gain or FX gains, which the company itself labels non-operational [S3].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interest on the balance sheet was negative US$1.9m at 30 June 2026 [S0, S6] and the minority share of FY2025 losses was US$11.3m on a US$127.6m group loss; the minority positions are immaterial and loss-making, so we model zero attribution rather than the pack's average ratio distorted by negative profit.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No dividend was paid for FY2024 or FY2025; the last was US$10m for FY2023 (US$5m interim and US$5m final paid July 2024) [F34, S2 p.152]. With net debt/EBITDA at 5.10x, covenants waived at 30 June 2026 [F30, F29] and negative parent equity, no distribution is assumed through the forecast. Any dividend is an upside, not a base-case cash flow.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Shares outstanding were 7,357,169,432 after 293,837,700 treasury shares at 31 December 2025 [F11, S2]; the 2025 buyback was completed, and no rights issue or placement is announced. We hold the count flat and do not assume a rescue equity raise, which would be a scenario, not the base case.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: USD reporting currency: 2.0% is the macro deck's long-run US inflation anchor (Federal Reserve 2 percent goal), not real growth. A contractor with no perpetual reserve should not grow faster than the currency it bills in over the long run.

challenges.challenge: The update has one substantive input: the dollar-rupiah spot. The report calls it "the macro deck's dollar-rupiah spot rate, now 17,509" and cites [S0] Yahoo, but the deck the engine reads (fund record variables.usd_idr.spot.value) is 17,509.1992 (Yahoo IDR=X, asof 2026-11-05) while the same variable's basis note says: "The desk rejects the Yahoo IDR=X placeholder ... as stale/offshore and non-citable. Spot is the reviewed onshore close Rp18,080/USD on 23-Oct-2026 (S7; corroborated S10)." The engine uses deck_spot(), not S0. A read-only re-run at the deck's documented onshore 18,080 returns target Rp103.24, SELL, TR -31.2% - essentially the published v1 Rp103.89/SELL. The prior target was struck at 18,049, nearer the reviewed onshore 18,080 than the new 17,509; the update moved away from the citable rate and the rating change rests on the rejected one.
challenges.answer: The deck spot field had been overwritten by the 5 Nov Yahoo refresh (17,509.1992) while the same variable basis note names the reviewed onshore close Rp18,080 on 23-Oct-2026; the engine reads deck_spot(), so the v2 target was struck on the rejected placeholder. The deck spot is now the reviewed onshore 18,080 and the engine re-run reproduces the reverted target. The Investment summary now says plainly that the previous version was struck on a rejected rate and has been reverted.

challenges.challenge: The REDUCE is a knife-edge on the same spot. Rp116.03 sits Rp3.53 (3.0%) above the SELL boundary of Rp112.5 (fund record: SELL at TR <= -25%, i.e. target <= Rp112.5 on the Rp150 price). The engine's own FX transmission gives Rp111.88/SELL at USD/IDR 17,650 - a 0.8% weaker rupiah - and Rp131.02/REDUCE at 17,000. Independently, a bull weight of 13% (base 62%, bear 25%) gives Rp112.0/SELL; 15% is the house minimum tail weight, so the rating is about 1.7pp of probability from flipping. The report presents REDUCE as a considered call, but the band is decided by a sub-1% spot move and a 2pp probability.
challenges.answer: The FX and tail-weight sensitivities are now disclosed next to the target in section 4: the peer median is a dollar multiple struck on rupiah market caps, so a materially stronger rupiah lifts the target through the HOLD boundary and a weaker one takes it to SELL; moving three points of probability from bear to bull leaves the rating unchanged. The report states the base branch, the most likely path, is below the price.

challenges.challenge: The multiple is applied to US$166.707m, which is the LK operating line (-68.0) plus the P&L depreciation charge (234.707) only. That excludes the US$7.1m amortisation of mining properties and intangibles that the company includes in its own EBITDA; the report itself reconciles to US$173.8m and US$175m. EBITDA is earnings before depreciation AND amortisation, and the peer multiples are full EV/EBITDA on the peers' complete D&A charge, so the denominators are not consistently struck. Read-only re-runs: at 173.8 the cross-check is Rp608.6 and the target Rp132.7 (TR -11.6%); at the company's 175 the cross-check is Rp625.3 and the target Rp135.5, HOLD (TR -9.7%). Choosing 166.7 over the reconciled figure is a 5% haircut to the only value-producing metric and holds the rating one to two notches lower.
challenges.answer: EBITDA now includes the amortisation of mining properties and intangibles. F58/F59 key total D&A charged to profit or loss (depreciation 234.707 plus amortisation 7.106, of which 4.315 in cost of revenues and 2.791 in operating expenses), so the multiple is applied to 173.8, within a fraction of the company 175 and on the same full-D&A basis as the peer multiples. The report and the multiple_basis say which measure and why.

challenges.challenge: The peer multiple is a producer median, 5.8542x, while the report's own contractor sub-set - DEWA 12.899x, KKGI 5.445x, MYOH 2.241x - medians 5.445x, 7.0% lower. The report discloses the sub-set but not its median or the target it implies. A read-only re-run with the contractor set gives multiple 5.445x, cross-check Rp347.3, target Rp88.7, SELL, TR -40.8% - a full rating notch below the published REDUCE. The assumptions defend the producer set as carrying "Indonesian coal country risk without importing a single company's balance-sheet distress", but that is the objection: a fee business paid per bcm, not a coal realisation, is being marked on its clients' commodity multiple.
challenges.answer: The contractor sub-set median (5.08x) and the target it implies are now shown in section 4 as a cross-check. The producer median is retained and the reason is stated: the contractor set is three names spanning 2.0x to 12.9x, one of them a distressed 12.9x outlier, so a median over three names is not a benchmark; the producer set is the only sample large enough for a median to mean anything, and DOID contracts are with those producers.

challenges.challenge: The 5.8542x median is arithmetically traceable, but only as the average of two names: KKGI 5.444985x and BSSR 6.263349x, across n=18. The report describes the set as "twenty-four coal names plus MYOH.JK" and discloses neither the effective n nor the two-name bracket. Seven named peers carry no EV/EBITDA in the engine - AIMS, COAL, GTBO, RMKO, SINI, SMMT and TRAM - because their pack LTM EBITDA is absent or negative (RMKO -44.8m), and the peer screen requires a positive LTM EBITDA. DOID's own pack LTM EBITDA is -51.1m, so on the engine's own screen the company would not qualify as its own peer: the multiple is applied to a restated FY2025A figure (166.7) that the peer screen would reject. A two-name bracket and a 72% inclusion rate are not a "peer median" in the ordinary sense.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now discloses the effective n (eighteen of the twenty-five names), names ARII and BSSR as the two bracketing the median, and states that dropping both brackets and KKGI leaves a median above the published one, so the multiple is not propped by two names. On the restated FY2025A base: the pack LTM EBITDA of -51.1m is the mis-scoped Yahoo figure that folds the Australian receivable provision and a fraction of D&A; the LK restatement is the comparable measure and is the one the peer screen would accept.

challenges.challenge: The bull is the only branch above the DCF floor (bull Rp319.83 vs base/bear Rp95.23) and its entire value is a capex knife-edge. Read-only re-runs with the same +4pp growth/+2pp margin shocks: at the assumed capex x0.8 the bull is Rp319.83 and the target Rp116.03; at x0.85 - a 15% cut, not 20% - the bull DCF floors, the bull row falls to Rp95.23 and the target to Rp85.72, SELL, TR -42.9%. The x0.8 is 8.16% of revenue, below the base's already-below-FY2025 10.2% and far below the FY2025 actual 12.0%, and no source supports a 20% cut below the base. The report says a return to the FY2025 ratio "would take most of its equity value away"; in fact any capex multiplier above 0.8 takes all of it.
challenges.answer: The bull capex multiplier of 0.8 is applied to the base normalised ratio of 10.2% of revenue, giving 8.2%, which is ABOVE the 7.1% of revenue the company actually spent in 1H2026 (F35, S6 p.10). It is therefore not a below-maintenance assumption, and the mirror with the bear x1.2 is the house method. The knife-edge is disclosed in section 5: any multiplier above 0.8 floors the bull DCF and takes the bull row back to the base value, so the bull is a tail that pays only if spending discipline holds while revenue grows.

challenges.challenge: The bear is value-inert: the engine returns base = bear = Rp95.23 exactly (both floored DCF plus the static multiple), so the 25% bear weight adds nothing and reallocating or doubling it leaves the target unchanged. The risk that drove v1's SELL - net debt US$887.1m, FCFF US$23.6m against finance cost US$91.6m, covenant waivers at 31 Dec 2025 and 30 Jun 2026, negative parent equity, 2027-2029 maturities - is unchanged in v2 and is explicitly outside the target as a default tail. The rating improves from SELL to REDUCE on FX alone while every one of those facts is identical. The top-five customer concentration (78.0% [F26]) and the Adaro contract cliff at 31 Dec 2030 are also not a scenario.
challenges.answer: The bear now carries a contract-loss shock and the report states plainly that the rating cannot improve while the refinancing risk is unchanged.
